conventions.convention: The finite field is part of the classical code data; a field of order q is not identified with Z/qZ for composite q. Classical codes have n ≥ 1 and permit logical dimension k = 0.
The finite-field dual uses the bilinear dot product Σ x_j y_j, without conjugation or positive definiteness.
Classical vectors are columns: G has shape n × k, H has shape (n−k) × n, ker H = C, and HG = 0; empty row and column shapes are allowed.
Classical distance is minimum nonzero weight for a nonzero code; for C = {0}, d(C) = n+1.
Quantum encodings use finite complex inner-product spaces with the root first-argument-linear pairing, logical dimension K ≥ 1, n ≥ 1 ordered physical factors, and projector P = VV*.

Operator weight is the minimum cardinality of a supporting factor set, using the declared wire permutation and identity on its complement; the empty tensor space is C and scalar identities have weight zero.
Detectability means PEP = λP for arbitrary endomorphisms E. For K ≥ 2, distance is the minimum non-detectable weight; for K = 1 it is the sentinel n+1. Detection alone asserts no recovery map.
With target factor order H_{σ(0)}, …, H_{σ(n−1)}, source factor i occupies target position σ⁻¹(i), so support S becomes σ⁻¹(S).

load_bearing.statement: For a linear isometry V between finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, V*V = I and P = VV* is the orthogonal projection onto im V. If K and N are the domain and codomain dimensions, 0 ≤ K ≤ N; K = 1 gives a line, and K = N gives the full codomain and P = I.
Let F be a finite field, n ∈ N, and D ≤ F^n have dimension r. Then D⊥ is a linear subspace of dimension n−r, and (D⊥)⊥ = D, including D = {0} and D = F^n.

For C ≤ F^n of dimension k, there are matrices G of shape n × k and H of shape (n−k) × n whose columns and transposed rows respectively form bases of C and C⊥, with ker H = C and HG = 0. This includes k = 0 and k = n.
E is supported in S if Π_S E Π_S⁻¹ = E_S ⊗ I_{Sᶜ} for some endomorphism E_S. Its weight is the minimum cardinality of such S.

Detectable operators form a complex linear subspace; replacing V by VU for a logical unitary leaves the projector, detectability and distance unchanged. For K = 1 every operator is detectable; for K ≥ 2 a non-detectable operator exists with weight at most n, every weight-zero operator is detectable, and distance lies in {1,…,n}.

For C ≤ F^n of distance d and t = floor((d−1)/2), every nonzero error of weight less than d has nonzero parity-check syndrome. If r = c+e with wt(e) ≤ t, c is the unique radius-t codeword candidate, and distinct weight-at-most-t errors have distinct syndromes. For a known erased set S with |S| < d, at most one codeword agrees with the received word outside S.
For a finite-register quantum code of distance d, every operator E with wt(E) < d is detectable: PEP = λ_E P for some complex scalar λ_E. No correction-map conclusion is asserted.
For a field F, n,k ∈ N and G ∈ M_{n×k}(F), independent columns imply that the image of x ↦ Gx is a k-dimensional linear subspace of F^n, including k = 0 and n = 0.

Existence of a specified classical encoding F^k → C, including k = 0.
Adjoint identities and the explicit quantum repetition projector calculation.
Real and imaginary components in the local polarization calculation.
Finite bases, dimensions, and zero-dimensional boundary cases.
Finite-field alphabet and field-order conventions.
Norm-preserving encodings and logical unitaries.
Linearity of matrix maps and encoding maps.
Classical code spaces, dual spaces, images and kernels.
Column-vector multiplication, syndromes, HG = 0 and empty matrix shapes.
Matrix shapes, coordinate indexing and degenerate shapes.
First-argument linearity, conjugate symmetry, positive definiteness and induced norms.
Row and column rank, dual matrices and parity-check nullspaces.
Finite-field vector-space structures used in classical code definitions.
Deriving V*V = I from equality of inner products.
Coordinate dimensions and standard bases, including the empty basis of F^0.
Self-adjointness of VV* and invariance under logical unitary changes.
Rank-one projection formulas under the first-linear pairing.

Dimension bounds, finite subspace bases and equality from equal dimensions.
Image dimensions, dual dimensions and dimensions of explicit parity-check kernels.
Dual-code dimension and the Reed–Solomon parity-check rank.
Identifying VV* as the orthogonal code projector.
Existence of the minimum nonzero classical codeword weight.
Field arithmetic in the binary and F_5 examples.

seams_checked.note: Opened the register, tensor-register, tensor-map, product-basis and wire-permutation suppliers. Ordered factors, empty tensor unit, first-linear pairing and inverse permutations are used faithfully; support transforms by σ⁻¹(S).

Clean injection, oblivious reflection, amplification identity and robust-isometry consumers use the general finite-dimensional isometry theorem only for J*J = I and the orthogonal projector JJ*. The supplier permits these spaces, including zero-dimensional cases.

Projector and subsystem consumers preserve the isometry identities. The distance corollary proves product support bounds and invokes a separate Knill–Laflamme recovery theorem; it does not infer correction directly from detection.

Checked bilinear-dual, parity-check, syndrome, support and code-projector uses. CSS correction retains 2t < d for the classical uniqueness argument, handles zero codes separately and uses additional recovery results for quantum correction.

Code-deviation spaces take the linear span of operators of bounded support. Channel-location schedules explicitly require Kraus operators supported on the declared factor set. Both uses match the local-operator support definition.
